ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: This study is reported according to the REporting of studies Conducted using Observational Routinely collected health Data for PharmacoEpidemiological research (RECORD-PE) reporting guideline 12 (checklist in appendix text S2) and was approved by the Health Research Authority (REC reference 22/PR/0095) and by the University of Bristol's Faculty of Health Sciences Ethics Committee (reference 117269).

In this respect, the present observational study more closely emulates the trial setting, as participants were drawn from primary care and a landmark new-user design was used to estimate the effect of starting metformin.

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> In this respect, the present observational study more closely emulates the trial setting, as participants were drawn from primary care and a landmark new-user design was used to estimate the effect of starting metformin.

Ethics approval statement:

> This study is reported according to the REporting of studies Conducted using Observational Routinely collected health Data for PharmacoEpidemiological research (RECORD-PE) reporting guideline 12 (checklist in appendix text S2) and was approved by the Health Research Authority (REC reference 22/PR/0095) and by the University of Bristol's Faculty of Health Sciences Ethics Committee (reference 117269).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

codebook_check.summary_text: We found no codebook or README documentation for the 236 extracted data columns.
report: This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.
We examined 2 codebook/README/label sources and 236 data columns across 100 files.
No codebook or README documentation was found, so no data columns could be matched to variable definitions.

#### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 1 file that software creates by itself, not the authors: editor settings (1). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 236 columns across 100 data files.
#### Issues Identified

48 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 100 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files. **1 data path was built at runtime** with `sprintf()`/`paste()`/`file.path()` instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author's own). #### Execution
**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 25 scripts: 4 ran without error, 17 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 4 were run by another script with `source()`. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **4 scripts stopped on a file another script writes**, so they were run once more after the other scripts: `cox_analysis.R` (covariates.R); `PPA_03_pooled_log_reg.R` (utility.R); `ps.R` (covariates.R); `treat_strat_feasibility.R` (metadates.R). Which script must run first can be stated in a README, or shown by numbering the file names (01_, 02_). **3 scripts looked for 3 files in another folder than the deposit has them**, so before running them once more we copied them there: `analysis/functions/utility.R` to `analysis/functions/analysis/functions/utility.R` for `fn_standardize_risks.R`; `analysis/covariates.R` to `analysis/analysis/covariates.R` for `data_process.R`; `analysis/metadates.R` to `analysis/analysis/metadates.R` for `PPA_02_add_events.R`. Building paths from the top of the project (as with `here::here()`), or keeping the folders the code expects, solves this.

text.text: Introduction: Observational studies report lower COVID-19 mortality among metformin users, but most used prevalent-user designs comparing long-term survivors with heterogeneous controls.
Randomised trials suggest little or no mortality effect.
No large observational study has used a newuser design to estimate the effect of starting versus not starting metformin on severe and Long COVID outcomes in adults with type 2 diabetes (T2D).
We aimed to estimate this effect on COVID-19-related hospitalisation or death, COVID-19 diagnoses, and Long COVID among adults with T2D in England.
Research design and methods: Using OpenSAFELY-TPP linked NHS electronic health records, we conducted a population-based cohort study with a landmark new-user design.

Adults aged 18-85 years newly diagnosed with T2D (August 2018-August 2019) were classified as starting metformin monotherapy within 6 months or not starting any antidiabetic drug, based on prescription data.
Followup began 6 months after diagnosis and before the UK pandemic (avoiding immortal time) for up to 2 years.
We estimated intention-to-treat and per-protocol effects using weighted Cox and pooled logistic regression, with negative (bone fracture) and positive (diabetes-related death) control outcomes.
Results: Of 52,341 eligible people, 19,599 (37.4%) started metformin.

For COVID-19-related hospitalisation or death, the maximally adjusted hazard ratio (HR) of metformin versus no antidiabetic was 1.17 (95% CI 1.02-1.35; 2-year risk difference 0.36%, 95% CI 0.09-0.62; intention-to-treat).
The per-protocol HR for COVID-19-related hospitalisation or death was 1.11 (95% CI 0.96-1.29).
The Long COVID estimate was imprecise (HR 1.39, 95% CI 0.83-2.33; intention-to-treat).

For bone fracture (negative control) the estimate was null (HR 1.00), but for diabetes-related deaths (positive control) it was elevated (HR 1.41, 95% CI 1.09-1.81), indicating unmeasured confounding.
The risks of severe and long COVID were slightly higher among people who started metformin, compared with those who did not start.
These results plausibly reflect unmeasured confounding.

These findings align more closely with randomised evidence than earlier prevalent-user studies and argue against a clinically meaningful benefit of starting metformin for COVID-19 prevention in newly diagnosed T2D.

Observational studies and their meta-analyses have consistently reported 30-40% lower COVID-19 mortality among metformin users, yet most used prevalent-user designs that compare long-term survivors with mixed control groups and can overstate benefit.
Randomised trials suggest little or no effect on mortality.

Using a new-user design in more than 52,000 adults with newly diagnosed T2D, risks of severe and long COVID were slightly higher among people who started metformin, compared with those who did not start.
These results plausibly reflect unmeasured confounding rather than harm.
These findings align with randomised evidence and argue against a clinically meaningful benefit of starting metformin for preventing severe or Long COVID in people with T2D.
They also illustrate how new-user designs can reconcile discrepant observational and trial results and should be prioritised in future drug-repurposing studies.
Metformin is a medication commonly used to treat type 2 diabetes.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, some studies suggested it might also protect against severe COVID-19, but many such studies had design limitations that could have made metformin look more beneficial than it truly is.

In this study, we used NHS health records from over 52,000 adults in England who were newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes to examine whether starting metformin shortly after diagnosis reduced the risk of being hospitalised or dying from COVID-19, being diagnosed with COVID-19.
We found no evidence that starting metformin protected against any of these outcomes, although the effect on long COVID was imprecisely estimated.
Our findings are consistent with results from clinical trials and suggest that metformin should not be expected to prevent severe COVID-19 in people with type 2 diabetes.

During the COVID-19 pandemic several drug repurposing candidates, including metformin, were investigated for their effect on COVID-19 outcomes. 1 Metformin is the most commonly prescribed firstline treatment for type 2 diabetes (T2D) and is an inexpensive, readily accessible medication with a well-known safety profile.
text.formatted: During the COVID-19 pandemic several drug repurposing candidates, including metformin, were investigated for their effect on COVID-19 outcomes. <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1</ref> Metformin is the most commonly prescribed firstline treatment for type 2 diabetes (T2D) and is an inexpensive, readily accessible medication with a well-known safety profile.

text.text: It has been hypothesized that metformin helps in preventing severe and long COVID-19 outcomes due to its anti-inflammatory and potential antiviral properties.

2,3   Several randomised trials, summarized in a recent meta-analysis, have evaluated the use of metformin to prevent severe COVID-19 outcomes among a broad at-risk population. 4 The metaanalysis concluded that metformin has little to no effect on mortality, but some (uncertain) effect on severe COVID-19 outcomes.
text.formatted: 2,3   Several randomised trials, summarized in a recent meta-analysis, have evaluated the use of metformin to prevent severe COVID-19 outcomes among a broad at-risk population. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> The metaanalysis concluded that metformin has little to no effect on mortality, but some (uncertain) effect on severe COVID-19 outcomes.

text.text: This is in contrast to results from observational studies and metaanalyses thereof, which generally reported 30-40% lower odds of mortality among metformin users compared with non-users. [5] [6] [7] [8] Importantly, most observational studies used prevalent-user designs to assess the effect of metformin rather than studying the effect of starting, compared with not-starting, metformin.
text.formatted: This is in contrast to results from observational studies and metaanalyses thereof, which generally reported 30-40% lower odds of mortality among metformin users compared with non-users. <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> Importantly, most observational studies used prevalent-user designs to assess the effect of metformin rather than studying the effect of starting, compared with not-starting, metformin.

text.text: Prevalent users are individuals who remain on long-term metformin therapy so are, by definition, survivors who tolerated the drug and maintained engagement with healthcare.
Therefore, comparing prevalent-users with non-users can over-estimate the benefit of treatment as former-users, who are less likely to have benefitted, are excluded.

For Long COVID, the evidence is more consistent: both randomised and observational analyses reported a protective effect of metformin on incident Long COVID. 9 To our knowledge, no large observational study focusing on adults with T2D has used a new-user design to estimate the effect of starting, compared with not starting, metformin among people with T2D on subsequent severe and Long COVID-19 outcomes.
text.formatted: For Long COVID, the evidence is more consistent: both randomised and observational analyses reported a protective effect of metformin on incident Long COVID. <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref> To our knowledge, no large observational study focusing on adults with T2D has used a new-user design to estimate the effect of starting, compared with not starting, metformin among people with T2D on subsequent severe and Long COVID-19 outcomes.

text.text: Such a design more closely mirrors the causal question addressed in randomised trials.
If metformin does confer protection, it would represent a widely available, low-cost intervention in a population at elevated risk of severe COVID-19.

We aimed to estimate the effect of starting versus not starting metformin on COVID-19 related hospitalisations or death, COVID-19 diagnoses, and Long COVID diagnoses, among adults living with T2D in England. openly for review and re-use under MIT open license (https://github.com/opensafely/metformin_covid/)
text.formatted: We aimed to estimate the effect of starting versus not starting metformin on COVID-19 related hospitalisations or death, COVID-19 diagnoses, and Long COVID diagnoses, among adults living with T2D in England. openly for review and re-use under MIT open license (<ref type="url" target="https://github.com/opensafely/metformin_covid/">https://github.com/opensafely/metformin_covid/</ref>)

text.text: We used a population-based cohort design (Figure 1).
text.formatted: We used a population-based cohort design (Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: People with a T2D diagnosis between August 1st, 2018, and August 1st, 2019 ('diagnosis window') were classified as starting or not starting metformin within 6 months after T2D diagnosis.
Follow-up started at 6 months after diagnosis ('landmark approach').

Because the latest possible date of T2D diagnosis (August 1st, 2019) was 6 months before the start of the pandemic in the UK (February 1st, 2020), no COVID-related outcomes could occur between T2D diagnosis and the start of follow-up.

Therefore, our design avoided creating 'immortal time' during which outcomes were excluded from analyses. 11 Follow-up ended at the earliest of: outcome, death, end of registration, maximum follow-up period (2 years) or administrative end of study (March, 1st, 2022 [end of systematic SARS-CoV-2 mass testing in the UK]).
text.formatted: Therefore, our design avoided creating 'immortal time' during which outcomes were excluded from analyses. <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11</ref> Follow-up ended at the earliest of: outcome, death, end of registration, maximum follow-up period (2 years) or administrative end of study (March, 1st, 2022 [end of systematic SARS-CoV-2 mass testing in the UK]).

text.text: People who died or were lost to follow-up (deregistration from the general practice) within 6 months after T2D diagnosis were excluded from analyses.

Eligible people had a T2D diagnosis within the diagnosis window, had been registered for at least 12 months before diagnosis with an English GP using TPP software, were aged between 18 years and 85 years at the time of T2D diagnosis, and had available data for sex, region, and area deprivation.
People hospitalized, in palliative care or a nursing home, with a missing glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) or a HbA1c above 75 mmol/mol in the 2 years prior to T2D diagnosis were excluded.

We excluded people with known history of hypersensitivity to metformin, moderate to severe renal impairment, or advanced decompensated liver cirrhosis, as well as people with prior use of metformin or another glucose-lowering medication (SGLT2, DPP4, sulfonylurea, thiazolidinedione, GLP-1, meglitinides, alpha-glucosidase-inhibitors, insulin) or any medication with metformin drug-drug-interaction potential (Cimetidine, hydroxychloroquine, tafenoquine, patiromer, ranolazine, Monoamine Oxide Inhibitors, Alpha-1 antagonists, Sotalol, Clonidine, Phosphodiesterase 5 inhibitors, Methyldopa, Prazosin, Terasozin, Doxazosin) in the past 14 days prior to T2D diagnosis (appendix text S1).

This study is reported according to the REporting of studies Conducted using Observational Routinely collected health Data for PharmacoEpidemiological research (RECORD-PE) reporting guideline 12 (checklist in appendix text S2) and was approved by the Health Research Authority (REC reference 22/PR/0095) and by the University of Bristol's Faculty of Health Sciences Ethics Committee (reference 117269).
The study protocol, including amendments and track changes, is available in the GitHub repository (https://github.com/opensafely/metformin_covid/tree/main/protocol).
text.formatted: The study protocol, including amendments and track changes, is available in the GitHub repository (<ref type="url" target="https://github.com/opensafely/metformin_covid/tree/main/protocol">https://github.com/opensafely/metformin_covid/tree/main/protocol</ref>).

text.text: We compared the treatment strategies 'start metformin monotherapy (i.e. no other antidiabetic drug) within 6 months of T2D diagnosis and continue metformin during follow-up unless a contraindication occurs' and 'do not start metformin or any other antidiabetic drug within 6 months of T2D diagnosis or any time during the follow-up'.
The exact drugs of interest are outlined in appendix table S1.
text.formatted: The exact drugs of interest are outlined in appendix table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S1</ref>.

text.text: Participants who started any antidiabetic drug other than metformin within 6 months of T2D diagnosis were excluded from analyses
The primary outcome was a composite of COVID-19-related hospitalisation and COVID-19-related death.
COVID-19-related hospitalisations, obtained from secondary care data including emergency care attendance, were defined as any (emergency) hospitalisation listing a COVID-19 diagnosis in any position.
Deaths were identified using linked ONS death registry data.
COVID-19-related death was defined as a death where the underlying or contributory cause on the death certificate was COVID-19.
If a person was hospitalised before death, the date of hospitalisation was used.

The secondary outcome 'COVID-19 diagnosis' was defined using an established algorithm combining any event indicating a COVID-19 diagnosis (i.e., a positive SARS-CoV-2 test, a COVID-19 diagnostic code in primary or secondary care, or a COVID-19-related death) in SGSS, SUS and ONS death registry. 13 The secondary outcome 'Long COVID' was defined using Long COVID diagnostic codes in primary care, introduced by the National Health Services in the UK, supplemented by viral fatigue codes. 14 In sensitivity analyses, we used diabetes-related deaths as a positive control outcome and hospitalisations due to bone fracture as a negative control outcome (appendix table S2).
text.formatted: The secondary outcome 'COVID-19 diagnosis' was defined using an established algorithm combining any event indicating a COVID-19 diagnosis (i.e., a positive SARS-CoV-2 test, a COVID-19 diagnostic code in primary or secondary care, or a COVID-19-related death) in SGSS, SUS and ONS death registry. <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13</ref> The secondary outcome 'Long COVID' was defined using Long COVID diagnostic codes in primary care, introduced by the National Health Services in the UK, supplemented by viral fatigue codes. <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14</ref> In sensitivity analyses, we used diabetes-related deaths as a positive control outcome and hospitalisations due to bone fracture as a negative control outcome (appendix table <ref type="table">S2</ref>).

text.text: Covariates identified as potential confounders included age (splines with knot locations based on 10, 50 and 90 percentile), baseline sex (binary), ethnicity (categorised as White; Black or Black British; Asian or Asian British; Other, including Missing and Mixed), deprivation (using the Index of Multiple Deprivation [IMD] -the official measure of relative deprivation for small areas in England defined by 7 domains, including income and barriers to housing and services; categories as 1 [most deprived] to 5 [least deprived]), rural/urban area (binary), smoking status (categorised as Never; Ever, including Missing; Current), health care worker (binary), GP-patient interactions in the year prior to T2D diagnosis (continuous), calendar time of T2D diagnosis (continuous), number of HbA1c measurements in previous 2 years (continuous) -all assessed at baseline.

Additional baseline covariates, which were also time-updated over the follow-up, included HbA1c (continuous), total cholesterol/high-density lipoprotein cholesterol ratio (categorised as below 3.5:1; 3.5:1 to 5:1; above 5:1; missing), prediabetes, diabetes-related complications, and binary indicators for fifteen comorbidities (appendix text S3 and appendix figure S1).
text.formatted: Additional baseline covariates, which were also time-updated over the follow-up, included HbA1c (continuous), total cholesterol/high-density lipoprotein cholesterol ratio (categorised as below 3.5:1; 3.5:1 to 5:1; above 5:1; missing), prediabetes, diabetes-related complications, and binary indicators for fifteen comorbidities (appendix text S3 and appendix figure <ref type="figure">S1</ref>).

text.text: Region was treated as a stratification factor (categorised into 7 regions: East, London, Midlands, North East and Yorkshire, North West, South East, South West).
We described demographic and clinical characteristics at T2D diagnosis date.
We generated a propensity score for receiving metformin for each individual, defined by the baseline covariates listed above, and examined how this differed by receipt of metformin.
We estimated both 'intention-to-treat' (ITT) and 'per-protocol' effects comparing the two treatment strategies.

To estimate the observational analogue of the ITT effect, we compared people who started metformin monotherapy within 6 months of T2D diagnosis with people who did not start metformin monotherapy or any other antidiabetic drug within 6 months of T2D diagnosis.
We fitted Cox models with calendar time scale and start of follow up 6 months after T2D diagnosis (the landmark date).
Follow-up ended at the earliest of the outcome, death or practice deregistration.
For each outcome, we estimated age-and sex-adjusted and maximally adjusted hazard ratios comparing the treatment strategies.
All models were stratified by region.
We estimated 2-year hazard ratios (HRs) with standard Wald 95% confidence intervals.

In addition, we used an inverse probability of treatmentweighted Kaplan-Meier approach to estimate the marginal (population-average) cumulative incidence of the primary outcome for each treatment group.
From these, we estimated 2-year risk differences (RDs) and risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals using the delta method.

To estimate the per-protocol effect, we artificially censored people in the no antidiabetic group who deviated from their assigned treatment strategy by starting metformin or any other antidiabetic more than 6 months after diagnosis of T2D.
We used inverse probability of treatment (with metformin or other antidiabetic drugs) weighting to account for this informative censoring.

To operationalize this, we discretised person-time into monthly intervals containing information on the time-updated covariate values at the beginning of the interval, treatment status during the interval, and whether the outcome event occurred in the next interval.
We used pooled logistic regression to estimate each person's probability of being treated in each interval, based on the baseline and time-updated covariates.
These were used to derive each person's cumulative probability of remaining uncensored during each time interval.

We calculated stabilised weights, for which the numerator was the probability of receiving the treatment that each individual received given their past treatment history (treatment, time variables, and baseline HbA1c as the strongest predictor), and we truncated them at the 1st and 99th percentiles (sensitivity analysis without truncation were also conducted).
We also used inverse probability of censoring weights, based on the same time-varying covariates, to account for potentially informative censoring due to deregistration from the general practice.

Finally, we fitted the outcome model, using pooled logistic regression on the discretised dataset, weighted by the product of the two weights above, and including linear and quadratic terms for month of follow-up to model the baseline hazard.
We fitted the outcome model with an interaction between time (month and month 2 ) and treatment.
We obtained 2-year HRs, cumulative incidence curves, 2year RDs and RRs, with 95% confidence intervals using bootstrapping.

We conducted subgroup analyses on the primary outcome by age group (below vs ≥60 years), sex (female vs male), ethnicity (white vs all other ethnicities combined), IMD (most deprived quintile vs other), BMI (obese vs overweight vs low/normal weight or missing), and HbA1c (below vs ≥59 mmol/mol).
We used Cochran's Q statistic to assess the differences within subgroups.
We conducted a sensitivity analysis restricting the study population to the propensity score region with substantial overlap (0.1-0.8).
We identified 54,341 people with T2D who met the inclusion criteria (figure 2).
text.formatted: We identified 54,341 people with T2D who met the inclusion criteria (figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">2</ref>).

text.text: Between T2D diagnosis and landmark (6 months later), 357 (0.7%) died, 1,143 (2.1%) were lost to follow-up and 711 (1.3%) started an antidiabetic treatment other than metformin.
Therefore, 52,341 people were included in the analyses.
Among these, 19,599 (37.4%) were prescribed metformin within 6 months of T2D diagnosis.

People who were prescribed metformin were younger (median age 58 [49-68] versus 64 [54-73] years) and had fewer comorbidities (for example, arterial hypertension: 9,441 [48%] versus 18,027 [55%]) than the no antidiabetic group (table 1).
text.formatted: People who were prescribed metformin were younger (median age 58 [49-68] versus 64 [54-73] years) and had fewer comorbidities (for example, arterial hypertension: 9,441 [48%] versus 18,027 [55%]) than the no antidiabetic group (table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: However, they had higher TC/HDL ratio (5:1 ratio category and above: 4,131 [21%] versus 4,953 [15%]) and higher HbA1c (59-75 mmol/mol category: 5,595 [29%] versus 1,659 [5%]).
Other characteristics were broadly similar across the groups.
The densities of the propensity score for those prescribed and not prescribed metformin had peaks at 0.3 and 0.25, respectively (appendix figure S2).
text.formatted: The densities of the propensity score for those prescribed and not prescribed metformin had peaks at 0.3 and 0.25, respectively (appendix figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">S2</ref>).

text.text: There was reasonable overlap between the groups across the entire propensity score distribution.

Characteristics of people who dropped out due to death or loss to follow-up before the landmark and before pandemic start were similar to those of people included in the study population (appendix table S3 and appendix table S4).

text.text: Overall, 375 (1.92%) of 19,599 participants in the metformin group experienced a COVID-19-related hospitalisation or death by 2 years follow-up, compared with 597 (1.82%) of 32,739 participants in the no antidiabetic group.

The cumulative incidence of COVID-19-related hospitalisation or death was 2.23% (95% CI 2.02% to 2.45%) in the metformin group and 1.87% (95% CI 1.72% to 2.03%) in the no antidiabetic group, with an absolute cumulative RD of 0.36% (95% CI 0.09% to 0.62%) and RR of 1.19 (95% CI 1.05 to 1.35) at maximum follow-up (appendix figure S4).

text.text: The Incidence of COVID-19related hospitalisation or death was higher in the metformin group (maximally adjusted HR 1.17, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.35; figure 3).

text.text: The adjusted 2-year RD for the per-protocol effect of starting metformin monotherapy vs never starting any antidiabetic drug on COVID-19-related hospitalisation or death was 0.21% (95% CI -0.08% to 0.51%).

The adjusted RR was 1.11 (95% CI 0.96 to 1.29) and the adjusted HR was 1.11 (95% CI 0.96 to 1.29) with no substantial change in estimates when censoring weights were not truncated (appendix figure S5, appendix table S5).

text.text: The incidence of COVID-19 diagnosis was slightly higher in the metformin than the no antidiabetic group (maximally adjusted HR 1.07, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.15, figure 3).
text.formatted: The incidence of COVID-19 diagnosis was slightly higher in the metformin than the no antidiabetic group (maximally adjusted HR 1.07, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.15, figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">3</ref>).

text.text: Within 2 years of follow-up, 33 (0.17%) of 19,599 participants in the metformin group had a recorded Long COVID diagnosis, compared to 33 (0.10%) of 32,739 participants in the no antidiabetic group (maximally adjusted HR 1.39, 95% CI 0.83 to 2.33, figure 3).

text.text: The subgroup analyses suggested some treatment effect heterogeneity for body mass index on COVID-19-related hospitalisation or death (appendix figure S6).
text.formatted: The subgroup analyses suggested some treatment effect heterogeneity for body mass index on COVID-19-related hospitalisation or death (appendix figure <ref type="figure">S6</ref>).

text.text: There was no evidence for effect modification by any of the other prespecified subgroups (age, sex, ethnicity, deprivation, or HbA1c).

Using a large, population-based cohort and new-user design, based on NHS electronic health records in England, this study estimated the effect of starting metformin within six months of T2D diagnosis on subsequent COVID-19 outcomes.
Among more than 52,000 adults with newly diagnosed T2D, we found no protective effect of starting metformin, versus not starting, against COVID-19-related hospitalisation or death.
Instead, after adjustment for an extensive set of confounders, starting metformin was associated with a slightly higher risk of COVID-19-related hospitalisation or death and COVID diagnoses.
Results for the positive control outcome analysis suggested residual confounding, although the null result for the negative control outcome (bone fracture) was reassuring.
Overall, the findings argue against a clinically meaningful benefit of starting metformin for prevention of severe or long COVID among people with T2D.
Recorded Long COVID diagnoses were rare, and estimates imprecise.

Observational studies -and meta-analyses thereof -have consistently reported lower mortality or reduced risk of severe COVID-19 among metformin users compared with non-users. [5] [6] [7] [8] [15] [16] [17] However, many of these studies were restricted to hospitalized populations and relied on prevalent-user designs, comparing long-term metformin users with heterogeneous control groups.
text.formatted: Observational studies -and meta-analyses thereof -have consistently reported lower mortality or reduced risk of severe COVID-19 among metformin users compared with non-users. <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref> However, many of these studies were restricted to hospitalized populations and relied on prevalent-user designs, comparing long-term metformin users with heterogeneous control groups.

text.text: Randomised trials, by contrast, have primarily evaluated starting metformin during the acute phase of COVID-19 in a broader at-risk population. 18, 19 A meta-analysis of these trials, as well as a large trial published after the meta-analysis, concluded that metformin has little to no effect on mortality and a small but uncertain effect on severe COVID-19 outcomes. 4, 19 Several factors may explain the discrepancy between observational and randomised evidence.
text.formatted: Randomised trials, by contrast, have primarily evaluated starting metformin during the acute phase of COVID-19 in a broader at-risk population. <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19</ref> A meta-analysis of these trials, as well as a large trial published after the meta-analysis, concluded that metformin has little to no effect on mortality and a small but uncertain effect on severe COVID-19 outcomes. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19</ref> Several factors may explain the discrepancy between observational and randomised evidence.

text.text: First, T2D itself is a strong risk factor for severe COVID-19, and improved glycaemic control achieved with metformin may influence disease course independently of any direct antiviral or anti-inflammatory effects. 20 While randomised trials largely excluded people with T2D -since they were already taking metformin and randomising them to metformin or placebo was unethical -observational studies were conducted mainly in the T2D population to satisfy the positivity assumption.
text.formatted: First, T2D itself is a strong risk factor for severe COVID-19, and improved glycaemic control achieved with metformin may influence disease course independently of any direct antiviral or anti-inflammatory effects. <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20</ref> While randomised trials largely excluded people with T2D -since they were already taking metformin and randomising them to metformin or placebo was unethical -observational studies were conducted mainly in the T2D population to satisfy the positivity assumption.

text.text: Second, observational studies predominantly included hospitalized patients, while randomised trials recruited individuals in the community with non-severe COVID-19.

Third, prevalent-user designs address the contrast of "being on metformin versus not being on metformin" at a given time, rather than the causal effect of starting metformin, which is the estimand targeted in randomised trials.

In this respect, the present observational study more closely emulates the trial setting, as participants were drawn from primary care and a landmark new-user design was used to estimate the effect of starting metformin.
The convergence of our results with randomised evidence underscores how design choices may explain some of the protective association seen in earlier observational work.
More broadly, this illustrates how new-user designs can help reconcile discrepant observational and trial findings, and should be prioritised in future observational drug-repurposing studies.

The currently available evidence on metformin and Long COVID suggests a potential protective effect. 9 Two randomised trials demonstrated that metformin started shortly after acute SARS-CoV-2 infection reduced incident Long COVID. 18, 21 A large observational analysis based on electronic health records from the US reported that prevalent use of metformin is associated with a reduced risk of Long COVID and an analysis based on English electronic health records -explicitly studying the starting of metformin after COVID-19 diagnosis -reported similar results. 22 In contrast to the previous UK study, we restricted our Long COVID outcome to coded diagnoses only -which was likely underreporting the scale of Long COVID 14 , and our estimates were too imprecise to draw meaningful conclusions.

text.text: This study has several limitations.
First, the landmark design introduces some concerns.
Date of eligibility (T2D diagnosis) and start of follow-up are misaligned.

In our specific case, however, selection bias at the landmark date due to differential outcome occurrence is impossible because the treatment allocation window closed before the pandemic began in the UK.

There may still be some residual selection bias due to depletion of susceptibles with regards to all-cause death, though only 1377 (2.6%) deaths and loss to follow-up occurred between T2D diagnosis and landmark date with similar characteristics between individuals who were excluded and those who remained in the analysis (appendix table S3).
text.formatted: There may still be some residual selection bias due to depletion of susceptibles with regards to all-cause death, though only 1377 (2.6%) deaths and loss to follow-up occurred between T2D diagnosis and landmark date with similar characteristics between individuals who were excluded and those who remained in the analysis (appendix table <ref type="table">S3</ref>).

text.text: Furthermore, estimates from this analysis have to be interpreted as conditional on still being alive at the time of reaching the six-month landmark.
Second, underreporting and misclassification of the outcomes (particularly Long COVID) is likely.
Possible misclassification of cause of death on death certificates cannot be excluded.
Misclassification of exposure is also possible since we only observed metformin prescriptions but not dispensing or intake.

Third, despite carefully defining a suitable study population with an indication for metformin (new T2D diagnosis with no contraindication to metformin, no extremely high HbA1c that would violate the positivity assumption) and adjusting for important confounders, unmeasured confounding is likely present, as suggested by the positive control outcome.

The bimodal propensity score distribution implies that the untreated group includes a substantial proportion of people with genuinely mild dysglycaemia who may be healthier in ways not fully captured by measured confounders, which is the most plausible explanation for the hazard ratio above one.
However, there was still reasonable propensity score overlap between the treatment groups, and estimates by HbA1c subgroups showed similar results.
A further source of residual confounding is changes in covariates (e.g.
HbA1c) between T2D diagnosis and the landmark date, when treatment status was assigned, because our models adjusted only for baseline values at T2D diagnosis.
Finally, our results apply only to the T2D population and may not generalise to other populations.

In summary, this study aligns more closely with randomised evidence than with earlier observational reports, reinforcing the conclusion that starting metformin should not be expected to reduce severe COVID-19 risk among people with newly diagnosed
T2D.

text.text: Primary care records managed by the GP software provider, TPP, were linked to the Office for National Statistics (ONS) death registration data, the national coronavirus testing records from the Second Generation Surveillance System (SGSS), the national vaccine register (National Immunisation Management System), and the NHS Secondary Use Service (SUS) data, through OpenSAFELY.
OpenSAFELY-TPP contains pseudonymised data of approximately 40% of the English population, including coded diagnoses, medications and physiological parameters.
No data from patients who registered a Type-1 Opt Out with their GP surgery were included in this study.
More information on the patients available for selection in the Service is available in the OpenSAFELY data page of the documentation.
The analysis dataset was defined and created using ehrQL (v1.0) / Python (v3.10).
Data management and analyses were conducted in R version 4.4.3.
For disclosure control, all counts were midpoint-6 rounded (https://docs.opensafely.org/outputs/sdc/).

text.text: The protocol, codelists and analysis code are shared
The data in the NHS England OpenSAFELY Analytics Service is drawn from General Practice data across England where Optum and TPP are the data processors.
This study uses data from TPP only.
Linked data from hospitals and death registrations are also available.

Access to the underlying identifiable and potentially re-identifiable pseudonymised electronic health record data is tightly governed by various legislative and regulatory frameworks, and restricted by best practice.
TPP developers initiate an automated process to create pseudonymised records in the core OpenSAFELY database, which are copies of key structured data tables in the identifiable records.
These pseudonymised records are linked onto key external data resources that have also been pseudonymised via SHA-512 one-way hashing of NHS numbers using a shared salt.

University of Oxford, Bennett Institute for Applied Data Science developers and PIs, who hold contracts with NHS England, have access to the OpenSAFELY pseudonymised data tables to develop the OpenSAFELY tools.
These tools in turn enable researchers with OpenSAFELY data access agreements to write and execute code for data management and data analysis without direct access to the underlying raw

OpenSAFELY has involved patients and the public in various ways: we developed a public website that provides a detailed description of the platform in language suitable for a lay audience (https://opensafely.org); we have participated in two citizen juries exploring public trust in OpenSAFELY; we have co-developed an explainer video (https://www.opensafely.org/about/); we have patient representation who are experts by experience on our OpenSAFELY Oversight Board; we have partnered with Understanding Patient Data to produce lay explainers on the importance of large datasets for research; we have presented at various online public engagement events to key communities (e.g., Healthcare Excellence Through Technology; Faculty of Clinical Informatics annual conference; NHS Assembly; HDRUK symposium); and more.

We will share information and interpretation of our findings through press releases, social media channels, and plain language summaries.
